methods.s_power: What a record this long can detect
methods.data_plain: Temperature and rain come from MERRA-2, a NASA model that blends many observations. For rain we also show GPM IMERG, a record from satellites and rain gauges, as a sensitivity check: the two share some inputs, so IMERG is not an independent confirmation. Every result says which kind of data it uses.
methods.data_experts: Region values are area-weighted means on each product's own grid (MERRA-2 0.5° × 0.625°; IMERG 0.1°), using the share of each cell inside the region. A region enters our set only when enough effective data cells cover it and only a small part of what its mean describes lies outside it. When two places are compared, a cell both touch goes to the one holding more of it, and each side must still keep enough cells. The screening map uses a conservative regrid to 1°. Input files are pinned by SHA-256 in the input manifest.
methods.seasons_plain: Months repeat every year: summers are hot and monsoons are wet. To see a long-term change we compare like with like: one value per year, or one per season (for example every June–September).
methods.seasons_experts: Temperatures use a day-weighted mean of the months; rain adds daily rate × days. A season and every rain total need all their months; a yearly temperature needs at least 10 of 12 months. Seasons that cross the new year are dated by the year in which they end. Space first, then time. Missing years stay missing; nothing is filled in.
methods.howmuch_plain: We draw the most typical slope through the years and say how much it changes per decade, with a 95% range: ranges made this way catch the true rate about 95 times in 100. It is not a 95% chance that this one range is right.
methods.howmuch_experts: Sen's slope (the median of all pairwise slopes, on actual years) with Conover's intercept. The range uses Sen's rank method with the Mann–Kendall variance inflated for memory and the multiplier 2.25 instead of 1.96: in our simulations 1.96 caught the true rate too rarely. The table shows how often each multiplier caught the true rate.
methods.significant_plain: A trend is “supported” when a pattern this clear would rarely appear from random ups and downs alone, after allowing for “memory” (a warm year is often followed by another warm year) and for the number of tests we ran.
methods.significant_experts: MK-AR1: Mann–Kendall with a tie-corrected variance, inflated by 1 + 2Σ(1 − k/n)φ̃ᵏ, where φ̂ is the AR(1) coefficient of a regression of each year on the year before, with an intercept and a trend (consecutive years only), bias-corrected as φ̃ = (nφ̂ + 2)/(n − 4) and clipped to [0, 0.95]. p uses the normal approximation with a continuity correction. A least-squares t-test with effective sample size is shown for comparison and never decides.
methods.domain_plain: We tested the method on many kinds of made-up records. It works well on some and badly on others, so we give verdicts only on the kinds where it works. Elsewhere we show the slope and say “no verdict: outside the range this method was tested for”. The table gives the largest year-to-year memory allowed for each record length.
methods.domain_experts: A verdict needs temperature or rain; the whole year or a pre-registered season; at least 20 complete years (15–19 are exploratory); no missing year; memory φ̃ at or below φ_max(n), the largest memory at which the calibrated false-alarm rate stays at or below 8%; and a pooled leftover-memory check across the region's data cells that finds no memory beyond what AR(1) describes. Stress tests: when the true trend is zero, records whose memory mixes a fast and a slow part, and AR(2) records, make any such test too eager; our domain checks lower those rates, and the table shows by how much.
methods.family_plain: Before we looked at any trend in real data, we wrote down and committed exactly which places, pairs, seasons and thresholds we would test. Only those tests get verdict words. Everything else is exploration.
methods.family_experts: The confirmatory family (for each pre-registered pair and each variable: both regions' yearly trends and the trend in their difference) uses Holm's correction; the secondary family of season tests uses Benjamini–Hochberg.
methods.compare_plain: “A trend here, none there” does not show that two places changed differently. We subtract one place from the other, year by year, and test the trend in that difference. Each place's own rate is shown beside it, never subtracted.
methods.compare_experts: The estimand is the trend in d(t) = A(t) − B(t), with its own Sen slope, range and MK-AR1 test; it is not Sen(A) − Sen(B). Labels: “opposite fitted directions” (descriptive only), “supported opposite trends” (both regions supported, opposite signs), “rates differ” (the difference is supported). Tested on made-up pairs with known answers:
methods.checks_plain: Before we accept a trend, we try to break it: a missing year, other start and end years, a change in the data rather than in the Earth.
methods.checks_experts: Coverage and gaps; documented data changes, each reviewed by a person for headline cases; leave-one-year-out; five other windows (robustness checks, not new claims). A doubt lowers the grade. The Pettitt test flags a sudden jump and never changes a verdict.
methods.grade_plain: Strong evidence: adjusted p below α/5 and no doubts. Supported trend: adjusted p below α and at most one doubt. Can't tell yet, which is not the same as no change: everything else. Whether the change is big enough to matter is answered separately, against a threshold declared in advance.
methods.power_plain: A short or noisy record can miss a real change. The table shows how often the test catches a trend of a given size (in standard deviations of the yearly noise, per year) in records of each length.
methods.power_experts: Power of MK-AR1 by simulation with an injected trend. The verdict card shows no “years needed” number.
methods.maps_plain: If you test thousands of places, some will look like trends by chance. We control the share of false alarms among the cells that stand out (false discovery rate 10%) and hatch the places we cannot test. The map is for exploring and gives no verdicts.
methods.maps_experts: Per 1° cell, MK-AR1 with memory pooled over the 5 × 5 neighbourhood and the leftover-memory check; Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.10 over the testable cells within each map.
methods.map_null_none: This build has no pure-noise map test.
methods.tests_plain: Golden tests assert values, tolerances and verdicts, and any mismatch fails the build.
methods.breaks_plain: Known changes in how each record was made. A person reviews each one that falls inside a headline case's years; the outcome is shown on that result.
methods.limits_plain: No forecasts. No claims about causes: at most, a result is “consistent with” a process. Linear trends only; jumps are flagged. Places smaller than the data cells are not in our set. Only temperature and rain get tested verdicts; water vapour and air pressure are shown as exploration layers, and other records are not in this release.
methods.reproduce_plain: Every result file is public and carries its build id, the input-manifest hash and the pre-registration hash. The same pinned inputs, pre-registration and code give the same files.

methods.leftover_title: Critical values of the leftover-memory check
methods.golden: This build: {passed} of {total} golden tests passed.

ai.lead: How we used AI tools to build this project, and where we did not use them.
ai.how_1: Planning: we asked many AI advisors (several models, each given a role such as statistician or skeptic) to critique our plan, had two research tools fact-check the claims, merged the advice by fixed rules, let our own simulation code settle every statistical dispute, and had a different model red-team the merged plan.
ai.how_2: Specification and engine: an AI assistant helped write our specification (documents, data formats, test cases with expected values) and wrote the statistics engine from it. The engine's numbers were checked against an earlier set of expected values, by simulation studies whose rules were fixed before they ran, and by tests that rebuild every example exactly.
ai.how_3: Code: AI coding assistants wrote the data pipeline and this website from that specification, checked by tests and read by a person.
ai.how_4: Language: AI drafted Bangla and English interface text, which a native Bangla reader checks.
ai.how_5: People decided the design, the statistical methods, every threshold, the regions and the comparisons, and we committed those choices before we looked at any real trend.
ai.product_title: AI in the product: the copilot only
ai.product_body: No AI computes, changes or decides any number or verdict: every value and verdict comes from one tested Python engine. The optional investigation copilot uses an AI model (Google's Gemini, or Anthropic's Claude, depending on the server's setup) to choose which evidence to open and to word its answers. It reads only this site's result files through fixed tools, and every number in its answers is checked against those files before it is shown; an answer that fails the check is replaced by a summary taken from the files.
ai.media_body: No AI-generated images, video or audio are used on this site.
ai.record_body: The repository keeps an AI-use statement and a log of every coding-agent session (docs/AI_USE.md and docs/ai_log/).

about.body_1: CaseFile Earth is a NASA Space Apps 2026 project for the challenge “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!”. It treats every trend as a case: it lines up the data that could answer a question, tests the trend, and shows a graded verdict or “can't tell yet”, with the evidence attached.
about.body_2: It covers Bangladesh, its divisions and nearby regions, in English and Bangla, and a 1° screening map of the whole planet for exploring. The site works offline from a single file.
about.role_a_body: Holds the methods, the pre-registration and the results build.
about.role_b_body: Builds the data pipeline from NASA archives and publishes the site.
about.role_c_body: Builds the screens, the watch cases and the words in both languages.
about.licence_data: NASA data: NASA open data; cite each record as listed on the Data & credits page.
about.licence_fonts: Fonts: Instrument Serif, Inter Tight, Noto Serif Bengali, Noto Sans Bengali and IBM Plex Mono (SIL Open Font License), bundled with the site.
about.licence_outlines: Map outlines: Natural Earth (public domain) through world-atlas (ISC). Earth image: NASA Blue Marble (public domain).
about.licence_libs: Libraries: React, globe.gl and three.js, Observable Plot, d3-scale-chromatic, Radix, Tailwind CSS, Motion and Zustand, each under its own open-source licence.
about.challenge_body: The challenge asks for a tool that helps people select Earth data, see how it changed, and say what changed, where, by how much and whether the change stands out from chance. CaseFile Earth answers it for temperature and rain, and tests the difference between two places directly.

any.title: Compare any two places
any.lead: Pick any two countries or regions and see them side by side, year by year. Exploration: the difference is not tested here; tested pairs have their own verdicts.
any.empty: Choose two places to see them side by side.
any.clock_title: The year's rhythm in both places

countrypanel.no_file: No yearly file for this place in this build.

story.title: The story of any place
story.lead: Pick any country or region and watch its NASA records play year by year: each yearly value, its stripes and the year's rhythm. Values, not tests.
story.intro: {place}, in {continent}: its yearly values from NASA's MERRA-2 records, {from} to {to}.
story.rhythm: The year's rhythm of {record}: highest in {peak}, lowest in {low}.
story.end: These are yearly values, not tests: a tested answer exists only for the pre-registered places. Open the full report to explore further.
story.what_1: A case is one question the engine answered, played as a short film on the real screens: the question, the place, the data, the test and the answer, step by step.
story.what_2: These three are the pre-registered headline questions, so every number in them comes from a tested result, including an honest "can't tell yet".
story.what_3: Below the cases you can also watch the story of any country or region: its yearly values, shown without a test.

trends.lead: How each NASA record is changing across the world, a continent or a country: every 1° square carries the engine's rate of change per decade, and this page counts them — how many rise, how many fall, and how many stand out after allowing for all the tests.
trends.headline: {scope}: {record} is rising in {up} and falling in {down} of {tested} tested squares since {since}.
trends.legend: Bar, left to right: rising and standing out, rising, falling, falling and standing out.
trends.histogram_note: How many squares change at each rate per decade (the engine's rate for each square; bars are counts).
trends.rank_lead: Each place with at least three tested squares. Its bar shows the share of its squares where {record} is falling (left of the middle line) and rising (right); the darker ends are squares that stand out after allowing for all the tests.
trends.note_squares: Squares are counted, not weighted by area: a 1° square near the poles is much smaller than one at the equator, and a country's squares are those whose centre lies inside its outline.
trends.note_tested: The counts above read the engine's screening map, square by square. The sections below run the engine's trend test once on the area-weighted yearly values of the world, each continent and each country (exploration). Only the pre-registered questions carry a graded verdict.
trends.note_missing: Sea level is not in this build: it needs another NASA record (sea surface height), which the data pipeline can add later.
trends.no_area: This build has no area series of {record} for this area.
trends.forest_title: Fastest rising and fastest falling countries
trends.forest_lead: The {n} countries where {record} rises fastest and the {n} where it falls fastest, each with its 95% range. Of {tested} countries tested, {out} stand out after allowing for all of them.
trends.forest_alt: Countries ranked by their trend per decade in {record}, with 95% ranges
trends.map_lead: Every country coloured by the engine's trend per decade in {record} on its area-weighted yearly values. Outlined countries stand out after allowing for all countries tested; grey ones have no test.
trends.map_alt: World map of countries coloured by their trend per decade in {record}
trends.hov_lead: Each row is a band of latitude, each column a year: the colour shows how far that band's average of {record} was from its {from}–{to} baseline.
trends.hov_alt: {record} by latitude and year, against the baseline
trends.rank_insight: In {n} of {total} places, more squares show {record} rising than falling.
trends.rank_legend: Bars: falling to the left of the middle line, rising to the right; darker at the ends = stands out after allowing for all the tests. Places with the same share are ordered by the share that stands out.

past.dash_lead: Every NASA record this build holds for {place}, side by side: the engine's trend test on its yearly values, the change between its first and last ten years, and its years as stripes. All of it is exploration: only the pre-registered questions carry a graded verdict.
past.dash_note: Click a record to open it below. "Stands out" means the trend passes the test after allowing for every place tested with the same record (false discovery rate under 10%); "doesn't stand out" means the test can't tell yet, not that nothing is changing. Each stripe is one year, from the record's lowest year (one end of its colour scale) to its highest (the other); hover a stripe for its value.
past.jump: The series has a possible jump around {year}, so a straight-line rate may not describe it well.
past.reason_descriptive: This record is not trend-tested: it is shown as values only.
past.reason_too_short: Too few years for a trend test (at least 15 are needed).
past.reason_missing_year: A year is missing, so the trend test is not run.
past.reason_constant: The values do not vary here, so there is nothing to test.
past.reason_not_finite: A trend test is not available for this series.
past.reason_phi_out_of_range: The years are too strongly linked to each other for the test's validated range, so it is not run.
past.no_trend_file: This build has not run the trend test for this record here.
past.then_lead: The same record seen six ways: its yearly values, its trend test, each year against the baseline, each month against its usual value, its first ten years against its last ten, and the trend month by month.
past.values_lead: Each year's mean, with the mean of the ten years up to it as a smoother line.
past.values_alt: {record} in {place}, yearly values and the ten-year mean
past.trend_method: The engine's Mann–Kendall test allowing for year-to-year memory, with the Sen slope and its 95% range, on the yearly values (exploration).
past.decade_sentence: In {place}, {record} averaged {a} {units} in {early} and {b} {units} in {late}: a change of {change} {units}.
past.anomaly_lead: Above the line: warmer, wetter or higher than the baseline average; below: lower.
past.anomaly_alt: {record} in {place}, each year's difference from the baseline
past.heatmap_title: Each month against its usual value ({from}–{to})
past.heatmap_lead: One row per year, one column per month. The usual seasonal cycle is taken out, so each square shows how unusual that month was.
past.heatmap_alt: {record} in {place}, each month's difference from its baseline average
past.dumbbell_lead: The average of each month in the first ten years and in the last ten years.
past.dumbbell_alt: {record} in {place}, monthly averages in the first and last ten years
past.months_lead: The engine's trend test run on each calendar month on its own. Darker bars stand out after allowing for all twelve months.
past.months_alt: {record} in {place}, the trend per decade of each calendar month
past.climograph_title: Temperature and rain through the year, then and now
past.climograph_lead: Month by month, the average temperature (lines, top) and the average rain (bars, bottom): one colour for the first ten years, one for the last ten.
past.climograph_alt: Temperature against rain by month in {place}, first and last ten years

challenge.title: Challenge this conclusion
challenge.intro: What supports this result and what could change it. Every line is read from the result file and names its source.

findings.test_supported: The test registered in advance supports it: adjusted p = {p}, below {alpha}. It is one of {n} tests written down before any trend was seen.
findings.test_cant_tell: The test registered in advance can't tell yet: adjusted p = {p}, above {alpha}. It is one of {n} tests written down before any trend was seen. That is not the same as no change.
findings.no_verdict: No verdict here: {reason}. The rate is shown, but no test decides it.
findings.sensitivity_role: This record is a sensitivity check. It is never graded, and it is not an independent confirmation.
findings.windows_agree: All {ran} alternative time windows agree with the main result.
findings.windows_disagree: Only {agree} of {ran} alternative time windows agree with the main result.
findings.loo_flip: One year matters a lot: leaving out {year} changes the answer.
findings.loo_ok: No single year changes the answer.
findings.jump_unreviewed: A jump around {year} stands out. No documented data change is recorded for it, and no person has reviewed it yet. A jump can come from the data rather than the climate, so treat the trend with care.
findings.jump_reviewed: A jump around {year} stands out, and a reviewed data change is recorded near it ({review}).
findings.break_documented: A documented data change ({year}) falls inside this window: {review}.
findings.coverage_doubt: Changes in data coverage over the record may affect the trend.
findings.practical_exceeds: The change is bigger than the size the team set in advance as worth reporting ({threshold} {units}).
findings.practical_overlaps: The range of the change overlaps the size the team set in advance as worth reporting ({threshold} {units}).
findings.practical_smaller: The change is smaller than the size the team set in advance as worth reporting ({threshold} {units}).
findings.exploration_up: The exploration screen marks this place as standing out (q = {q}). That screen compares many places with a different correction. The test registered in advance, above, is the one that decides.
findings.exploration_down: The exploration screen does not mark this place as standing out. That screen compares many places with a different correction. The test registered in advance, above, is the one that decides.
findings.other_unmatched: A second record of the same quantity covers {first}–{last}, not {mainFirst}–{mainLast}. Its rate ({rate} per decade) is not a matched comparison, and it is a sensitivity check, not a confirmation.
findings.other_matched: A second record of the same quantity, over the same years, gives {rate} per decade. It is a sensitivity check, not a confirmation.
findings.rates_differ: The test supports that the two places changed at different rates.
findings.rates_same: The test does not show that the two places changed at different rates.
findings.opposite_fitted: Their fitted lines point in opposite directions.
findings.opposite_supported: Both places have supported trends, in opposite directions.
findings.split_ok: The two places are compared on separate data squares, so neither borrows the other's data.
findings.split_fail: The two places share too many data squares for a clean comparison.

windows.title: The rate in each time window
windows.note: Dot: rate per decade. Line: its 95% range. The main window is drawn darker; the others start later or end earlier.
windows.alt: Rate per decade in the main window and {n} alternative windows

class.exploratory_note: Shown for exploration: no verdict, and no test registered in advance.
class.descriptive_note: Values as recorded, without a test of change.

panel.title: Investigation copilot
panel.intro: Ask about a place or a record. Answers come only from this site's NASA result files, and the evidence opens beside this panel.
panel.placeholder: Ask about a place, a record or a result…
panel.ai_note: AI-written text. Every number and verdict comes from the result files and is checked before it is shown.
panel.checked: Numbers checked against the result files.
panel.replaced: The written answer did not pass the checks, so this summary from the result files is shown instead.
panel.unavailable: The copilot is not available here: it needs the site's server, which this copy does not have. Everything else works, and the ask box on the map answers many questions without it.
panel.checking: Checking whether the copilot is available…

watch2.way_cases_body: A registered investigation played on the real screens, step by step, ending in its verdict or in "can't tell yet".
watch2.way_story_body: Pick any country or region and watch its records play year by year. Values, not tests.
watch2.why: The globe answers one place at a time and the copilot answers in words. A case shows the whole reasoning: what was fixed in advance, what the data say, which checks it passed, and why the answer is what it is.
